strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the paper targets MLLM hallucination via RL post-training and provides a coherent narrative linking outcome-only rewards to spurious background correlations and hallucinations.

Extensive empirical evaluation across a broad suite of benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, MME, GPT-4o assisted eval, V*, HR-Bench 4K/8K, refCOCO/+/g, ReasonSeg, and multiple math/reasoning benchmarks), plus ablations on reward components, hyperparameters, GRPO variants (DAPO, Dr.GRPO, GCPO), decoding modes, and implementation paths. This is unusually thorough for a single submission.

The proposed causal completeness reward (sufficiency + necessity) is a reasonable, well-formalized token-level signal, and the integration into the GRPO advantage function is described with sufficient detail (equations, pseudo-code in the appendix).
Results are consistent across four different base MLLMs (InstructBLIP, MiniGPT-4, LLaVA-1.5, Qwen-VL) and on top of Qwen2.5-VL-7B, suggesting the method is not model-specific.

The empirical finding that MLLMs exhibit broader gradient saliency over task-irrelevant background compared to text-only LLMs under identical GRPO training is an interesting observation that motivates the method, even if not conclusive.
The paper is generally well-written, with clear figures (Figures 4, 6, 9, 10) illustrating the reward computation and its qualitative effect.
weaknesses: The causal framing is overclaimed relative to what is actually implemented. The 'causal sufficiency' and 'causal necessity' scores are essentially counterfactual-sampling-based token attribution heuristics, not a principled causal inference procedure. The SCM in Figure 3 is a high-level schematic and does not constrain the optimization in a way that would justify strong causal language.

The central empirical claim (that outcome-based GRPO rewards induce spurious background correlations that cause hallucinations) rests primarily on gradient saliency visualizations, which are known to be noisy and only loosely correlated with model reasoning. The LLaVA-vs-LLaMA 'toy experiment' is suggestive but does not establish the causal chain asserted in contribution (i).

Computational overhead is not adequately accounted for. Computing the causal completeness reward requires H=8 continuations per token plus masked generations, and the 'training time' axis in Figure 12 is relative and does not clearly separate the cost of generating causal rewards from policy optimization. A compute-matched comparison against standard GRPO would strengthen the claim that the gains come from the causal reward rather than extra sampling.

The sufficiency score formulation (Eq. 6) and the comparison between r(Ỹ_t) and r(Ỹ_{t-1}) are somewhat ambiguous, and the necessity score (Eq. 7) relies on a single masked generation, which may be noisy. It is unclear how sensitive the reward is to these design choices beyond the H ablation.

The improvements, while consistent, are sometimes small in absolute terms (e.g., CHAIR_S 19.8 vs. 21.5 for GCPO on LLaVA-1.5), and it is not fully established that these margins are statistically significant.

The related-work discussion of causal methods for hallucination (e.g., GCPO [17], which also uses causal structure in policy optimization) is somewhat thin, and the differentiation from the most closely related causal RL baseline could be sharper.

The claim that the method 'mitigates hallucinations' by promoting causally sufficient/necessary tokens would be more convincing with an analysis isolating hallucination-specific effects (e.g., does COPO reduce hallucinations on background-heavy images specifically, as the motivation predicts?).

strengths: The paper targets a well-motivated and practically important problem—hallucinations in MLLMs—and proposes a novel angle: injecting token-level causal sufficiency/necessity constraints into the GRPO post-training objective to counteract spurious background–answer correlations.

The empirical motivation (Figure 2, Figure 8) comparing gradient saliency of an MLLM (LLaVA) versus a text-only LLM (LLaMA) under identical GRPO training is a compelling and intuitive diagnostic that spurious background reliance is stronger in the multimodal setting.

The method is cleanly formulated and demonstrably plug-and-play: Table 9 shows COPO consistently improves three different GRPO variants (DAPO, Dr. GRPO, GCPO) on CHAIR_S, CHAIR_I, and POPE, which strengthens the generality claim beyond a single baseline.

Evaluation breadth is strong and includes hallucination benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE), MME text quality, GPT-4o-assisted caption evaluation, high-resolution V*/HR-Bench, grounding (refCOCO/refCOCO+/refCOCOg/ReasonSeg), and reasoning/math (MathVista, MathVerse, WeMath, DynaMath, LogicVista), all with reported deltas over SOTA.

Ablations are thorough and directly support the design: component ablation (S_suff vs. S_nec, Table 3), hyperparameter sensitivity (Figures 7, 11), decoding-mode robustness (Table 8), implementation-path comparison (Table 10), and a training-time/performance trade-off analysis (Figure 12).

The qualitative analysis (Figures 6, 9, 10) showing gradient saliency shifting from background to foreground and token-level causal rewards becoming concentrated on evidence-bearing tokens provides interpretable support for the mechanism.
The paper is clearly written, with good figures and a well-organized appendix that documents notation, pseudo-code, baselines, and benchmarks, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The 'causal' framing is somewhat looser than the terminology suggests. The causal sufficiency/necessity scores (Eqs. 6–7) are essentially single-token masking/attribution heuristics (reward with vs. without the token), not rigorous causal identification of L_c vs. L_s as the SCM implies. The SCM (Figure 3) is used descriptively rather than to derive testable identification claims, so the gap between Definition 3.1 and the actual reward implementation is not fully bridged.

The sufficiency formulation in Eq. 6 is unusual: it multiplies the mean reward difference by an indicator I(r(Ỹ_t) > r(Ỹ_{t-1})), effectively zeroing the score when the condition fails. Combined with r_causal = λ_s S_suff + λ_n S_nec, tokens with negative causal contribution receive 0 rather than a negative signal, which may limit the ability to actively suppress spurious tokens. The motivation and behavior of this rectified formulation should be discussed more carefully.

The necessity score relies on a single masked forward pass per token (Eq. 7) and, per the authors, deliberately avoids sample averaging—a noisy estimate that may not reliably capture indispensability. The sufficiency score requires H extra samples per token (H=8 used), and no clear accounting of the added training/inference cost is given in the main text, despite Figure 12.

The motivating comparison between MLLM and LLM (LLaVA vs. LLaMA) conflates modality with architecture/data and uses different input types (image vs. textual description), so the attribution of the gradient-saliency difference specifically to 'spurious background correlation' is suggestive rather than cleanly established. The authors themselves hedge with 'we speculate.'

Novelty relative to prior causal/PNS-based work (e.g., [73] invariant learning via sufficient and necessary causes, [75] causal CoT reasoning) is moderate; the core mechanism is a reward-shaping variant over GRPO, and the paper would benefit from a sharper delineation of what is conceptually new beyond combining existing ideas.

Some main-text tables mix absolute scores with deltas (Table 1) in a way that can obscure which baseline corresponds to which backbone, and comparisons to close causal competitors (GCPO) would be clearer if placed side-by-side within a single framework rather than spread across tables.

The causal claims would be stronger if the paper provided a direct intervention-style validation (e.g., controlled insertion of background-only cues) to show that reducing L_s dependence causally reduces hallucination, rather than relying on aggregate benchmark improvements.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem: hallucination in multimodal LLMs and the limitations of outcome-only GRPO-style post-training.
It proposes a concrete token-level causal completeness reward that combines sufficiency and necessity scores and integrates them into GRPO, yielding a clear algorithmic pipeline.
The empirical observation that MLLMs can show gradient saliency on background regions under GRPO is interesting and provides useful motivation for studying spurious correlations.

The experimental evaluation is broad, covering hallucination benchmarks (CHAIR/POPE), high-resolution understanding, grounding, and mathematical/reasoning benchmarks, with consistent gains over many strong baselines.

Ablations on sufficiency/necessity components, different GRPO variants, parameter sensitivity, and decoding modes give some evidence that the proposed reward components contribute to the final performance.
weaknesses: The causal framing is not rigorously established. The SCM in Figure 3 makes strong, unjustified assumptions (e.g., Y -> L_c and treating background as non-causal), and the operational scores in Eqs. 6-7 do not actually implement the probabilities in Definition 3.1.

The motivating MLLM-vs-LLM comparison is confounded. The LLM receives a textual description of the image, so the absence of background pixels/tokens does not demonstrate that GRPO causes spurious background correlations; architecture, pretraining, and input modality are uncontrolled.

Gradient saliency is not causal evidence. High saliency on background regions may reflect scene context or visual-encoder properties, and there is no before/after GRPO or supervised-fine-tuning control to attribute the effect to outcome-based rewards.

The proposed optimization is essentially heuristic reward shaping. Adding r_causal to the group-normalized advantage (Eq. 9) can flip the sign of advantages for bad trajectories and does not directly optimize the stated causal objective; no theoretical analysis connects Eq. 11 to causal completeness.

The necessity intervention is weak. Replacing a token with a zero embedding is an out-of-distribution perturbation rather than a valid removal intervention, and Eq. 7 uses only a single sample while sufficiency uses H samples, making the necessity score noisy and inconsistent.

Key experimental controls are missing. There is no clear vanilla GRPO baseline in the main results, no random/entropy token-level reward baseline, and no control for reasoning length, so the gains may come from generic reward shaping or longer chains rather than causal token selection.

Reproducibility is insufficient. The reward function r(.) for open-ended captioning and the training data are not specified; the claimed 'offline' GRPO setup with pre-collected trajectories conflicts with on-policy GRPO/importance sampling, and code is only promised in supplementary materials.

Evaluation has limitations. CHAIR/POPE use only 500 images, no significance tests are reported, and some baselines/backbones are not matched in training data or compute, making the comparisons less conclusive.

The paper is difficult to verify from the main text: critical details (training data, reward model, prompt formats, handling of non-VQA tasks) are relegated to an appendix, while the main method section is compressed and notation-heavy.
